The “Input Description” table (Section 3 of the TEXTILE manual) enumerates and briefly defines the ten core record types and subsections you must supply to drive the membrane‐cutting algorithm.  Each subsection corresponds to a keyword or record group in the TEXTILE input deck.  Below is a structured, detailed breakdown suitable for ingestion into a RAG‐enabled vector store:

1.  Input Language (3.1)  
    • Defines the overall syntax and grammar.  
    • Specifies whether free‐format or fixed‐format record styles are used.  
    • Establishes comment conventions, continuation rules, and case‐sensitivity.  

2.  Input Records (3.2)  
    • Describes the generic record structure shared by all modules.  
    • Details field widths, delimiters, optional versus mandatory columns.  
    • Explains error‐checking behavior and record‐type codes.  

3.  CTRL – Control of the Analysis Method (3.3)  
    • Top‐level control card for selecting the surface development approach (e.g. geodetic vs. minimal‐energy).  
    • Flags for global parameters: prestress activation, iteration limits, convergence criteria.  
    • References to material property sets and boundary conditions.  

4.  PREP – Prepare Sofiplus/AutoCAD Cutting Lines (3.4)  
    • Conversion and formatting of native CAD‐derived edge geometry.  
    • Options for snapping, smoothing, and meshing the input lines before surface development.  
    • Output directives for DXF, DWG or native Sofiplus formats.  

5.  CUTT – Cutting Pattern (3.5)  
    • Core command block that drives the actual flattening of the curved membrane.  
    • Parameters for patch segmentation: max. element size, allowable shear distortion.  
    • Options for automated or manual patch numbering and labeling.  

6.  GRP – Group Control (3.6)  
    • Defines logical collections of patches or assemblies (e.g. roof bays, sail segments).  
    • Enables batch processing of identical patch groups.  
    • Controls stacking order and seam‐matching rules across group boundaries.  

7.  QUAD – QUAD Elements (3.7)  
    • Specification of quadrilateral finite‐element mesh layout.  
    • Input of node connectivity, aspect‐ratio constraints, and element orientation flags.  
    • Toggles for mesh refinement, transition zones, and local grading factors.  

8.  COMP – Compensation (3.8)  
    • Material‐specific stretch compensation parameters.  
    • Inputs: warp/weft modulus, Poisson’s ratios, pre‐tension levels.  
    • Algorithmic options: isotropic vs. orthotropic compensation, iterative vs. direct.  

9.  LINE – Cutting Lines (3.9)  
    • Definition of final cut edges, seam allowances, overlap tolerances.  
    • Offsetting commands: constant offset, variable offset based on curvature.  
    • Labeling and annotation flags for CNC export or plotting.  

10. ECHO – Output Extent (3.10)  
    • Controls verbosity of the run‐time listing and input echoing.  
    • Toggles detailed logging of meshing steps, compensation corrections, and error‐checks.  
    • Options for selective echo by module or record‐type code.  

By indexing each of these subsections—along with their key parameters, flags, and expected input formats—your RAG‐powered retrieval system will be able to surface precise guidance and examples whenever a user query references a specific TEXTILE input record.

 TEXTILE calculates the development of a 3D-curved surface. It includes the compentation of the stressed membrane to obtain the cutting pattern areas.

The image presents two side-by-side renderings of a membrane formfinding model, illustrating the transition from an initially folded input geometry (left) to the final prestressed equilibrium shape (right). Both views share the same boundary conditions, mesh topology and supporting geometry, but differ in their internal stress definitions and resulting surface form.

Left View (“Folded Input System”):
- A six-cornered base outline sits on the ground plane, with each corner marked by a small red square denoting pinned supports.  
- From these six supports, a light-blue, quadrilateral mesh rises toward a central elliptical ring at the top. The mesh is initially folded along straight lines, creating a faceted, almost conical tent-like shape with sharp ridges.  
- The central ring is depicted in yellow and has an oval opening; four equally spaced stiffeners (vertical struts) connect it down to the mesh, but they carry no active tension or compression in this initial state.  
- The mesh panels are flat between the fold lines, showing a uniform coloration of pale cyan. Grid lines emphasize the segmentation into rectangular patches, and the entire form appears largely governed by the input geometric constraints rather than any internal prestress.

Right View (“Stressed Membrane”):
- With a prestress definition applied, the mesh relaxes into a smooth, doubly curved surface. The color palette shifts subtly: areas of higher membrane tension near the ring appear in deeper blue, transitioning to lighter cyan down toward the supports.  
- The previously sharp ridges have rounded out into gentle curvature, giving the form a more organic, minimal-surface character. The mesh still follows the same quadrilateral network, but each panel is now warped in three dimensions.  
- The yellow ring and vertical struts are now visibly loaded: the ring maintains its geometric shape while the struts carry compression back down into the membrane.  
- Each red support remains fixed, anchoring the edges of the membrane. The overall form is in static equilibrium, with internal tension balancing the boundary reactions and strut forces.

Contextual Note:
This side-by-side comparison encapsulates the critical “formfinding” step in tensile membrane design. By assigning different prestress levels (e.g., uniform surface tension or varying edge tensions), the initially folded geometry deforms into distinct equilibrium shapes. Such prestress definitions are essential preconditions for generating cutting patterns: without achieving this balanced, curved membrane form, downstream tasks like pattern flattening or fabrication layout cannot proceed accurately.

Necessary precondition for a cutting pattern is the formfinding. The formfinding has to create a stressed system in equilibrium. In this step, different prestress definitions will produce different membrane forms.

The image shows a three-dimensional view of a tensile membrane structure with its geodetic cutting lines superimposed. At the core of the membrane is a large circular opening (a “crown ring”), from which a family of red curves (the geodetic lines) radiate outward toward the membrane’s boundary. Those red lines represent the shortest paths on the curved surface between two points and are the prescribed cutting lines needed to produce flat textile panels.

Key elements in the rendering:

  • Membrane geometry  
    – The surface is a single-layer shell, modeled with a network of quadrilateral elements (a quad mesh). Visually, the mesh is indicated only faintly, allowing the cutting lines to stand out.  
    – The membrane has a saddle-like, anticlastic shape: it rises to the circular opening at its apex and then slopes downward in all directions to a closed perimeter.  

  • Boundary and opening  
    – The outer edge of the membrane is drawn in yellow dashed lines. This boundary is non-planar but appears projected onto a single plane for visual clarity.  
    – The inner circular “vent” or opening at the apex is also outlined in yellow.  

  • Geodetic cutting lines  
    – The geodetic (shortest-path) curves are displayed in red. Each line begins at a point along the circular opening (marked in green) and proceeds along a uniquely computed geodesic to a corresponding point on the outer boundary.  
    – The lines are essentially “ribs” dividing the surface into panels that, when cut and laid flat, will form textile segments with minimal distortion.  
    – At certain key nodes (e.g. the start/end of each geodetic), green circular markers and small numeric labels indicate the node numbers or load-case identifiers used by the cutting-pattern software (WINGRAF).  

  • Visualization conventions  
    – Yellow: all fixed boundaries (inner and outer edges).  
    – Red: computed geodesic cutting lines (TEX​TILE CUTT output).  
    – Green: special markers denoting control points or group-limit activations in the WINGRAF editing menu.  
    – The surface is lightly shaded (white to gray) so that the curvature is visible but the mesh lines remain unobtrusive.  

  • Software context  
    – This view is typical of the WINGRAF environment after executing the “Textile cutting analysis” step. It confirms that the .tex file was read successfully and that the geodetic lines are correctly projected onto the quad-element membrane.  
    – In practice, one would export these red curves as DXF via ASE-STOR-SPEI-CUTT or the SOF_G_exportcuttinglines routine in SOFIPLUS-AutoCAD, then reimport the cutting areas back into SOFIPLUS for final panel generation.  

Overall, the figure provides a clear 3D illustration of how geodetic lines subdivide a curved membrane into manufacturable, flat-pattern textile pieces. The color coding and node markers assist the engineer in verifying that the correct load case and group limits have been used to generate an accurate cutting pattern.

The image is a color‐coded 3D rendering of a thin membrane or shell with an oval central opening, viewed from a slightly elevated “ground” perspective.  It illustrates how a complex surface has been subdivided into discrete cutting areas by a network of so-called geodetic lines.  These cutting areas are each rendered in a unique hue so that their boundaries stand out clearly against one another, and within each area a fine triangular mesh is overlaid to emphasize the underlying finite-element discretization.  According to the accompanying caption (“Figure 2.3: 3D-cutting areas: shown in a ground view”), these subdivisions have been both defined and automatically numbered by a software package called WINGRAF.  

Overall layout  
• The outer shape is roughly a warped rectangle, whose four edges curve slightly in and out, giving the form a gentle saddle-like appearance.  
• Cut out from the center of this surface is an approximately oval opening. The shape of the outer boundary and the central hole suggest a doubly‐curved shell, though only its “floor plan” projection is shown here.  
• Radiating from the rim of the central opening toward the outer perimeter are a series of wedge-shaped sectors. These sectors vary in angular width but share the common characteristic that each is defined by two bordering geodetic curves.  

Color and meshing  
• The sectors are colored in a repeating palette of vivid primary and secondary colors—bright red, deep blue, forest green, golden yellow, teal, orange, light cyan, and lime green. Adjacent sectors never share the same color, ensuring each region is visually distinct.  
• Within each colored zone, a fine triangular mesh is drawn in thin dark gray or black lines. The mesh triangles are not uniform in size: they become smaller and more concentrated near the inner boundary (around the oval cut-out) and coarser toward the outer perimeter. This reflects a typical adaptive meshing strategy where higher resolution is needed around curved or load-intensive features.  
• The geodetic lines themselves—the boundaries between cutting areas—are highlighted by slightly thicker and darker segments of the mesh. These curves curve smoothly across the surface from the inner opening to the outer edge, following the shortest (geodesic) paths in the 3D shell geometry.  

Numbering (not shown)  
• Although the individual sectors are said to be numbered in the WINGRAF program, the figure as presented does not display explicit numeric labels. One can infer, however, that each colored wedge corresponds to a unique identifier used later in the software for toolpath generation, manufacturing sequencing, or stress analysis.  

Visual impression and purpose  
• The result is a visually striking “pie-chart” arrangement deformed to match the curvature of a 3D surface. It conveys at a glance how a complex doubly curved form can be partitioned into manageable sub-regions for downstream processing.  
• The combination of clear color coding, smooth geodesic boundaries, and detailed triangular meshing makes it easy for an engineer or researcher to verify the layout of cutting zones, check mesh quality, or plan assembly and fabrication steps.  

Contextual note  
• This type of visualization is typical in advanced CAD/FEM environments. By defining geodetic cut lines, one ensures that each panel or patch follows minimal‐strain paths, which is crucial when fabricating shells from composite materials or when programming automated machining centers.  
• The image thus serves as both a design verification tool and a communication artifact, summarizing complex geometric and meshing information in a single, readily interpretable graphic.
The geodetic lines define the cutting areas in the 3D space. The cutting areas are determined and numbered in the program WINGRAF:

This diagram presents an “exploded‐view” layout of flattened 2D cutting panels that have been generated by TEXTILE from an originally curved 3D surface. The panels have been moved radially outward—like slices of a pie—so that none overlap, and each is labeled with its panel number (“Nr = …”) in small blue text. A roughly square void remains at the center, emphasizing that these pieces once formed a continuous tubular or ring‐shaped 3D surface.

Key visual elements:

 • Arrangement and count  
   – There are about 27 individual panels, each oriented at a slightly different angle around the center.  
   – The panels alternate around the full circle, giving a starburst or gear‐wheel impression.  

 • Shape and geometry  
   – Each panel is a four-sided, slightly trapezoidal or quadrilateral shape whose width and taper vary from one piece to another.  
   – The outer boundaries of all panels are drawn with fine dashed lines; these represent the “stressed,” ironed‐flat form, which exactly preserves the original 3D area.  
   – Superimposed on each dashed outline is a filled, solid‐color version of the same panel—this is the “relaxed” form, after the material’s internal stresses have been released and the area shrinks slightly.  

 • Color coding  
   – Panels are individually colored in a repeating palette (e.g. bright red, deep blue, cyan, lime green, yellow, teal).  
   – The fill color matches the dashed‐line color, helping to link each relaxed shape back to its original stressed outline.  

 • Legend and caption  
   – Although there is no formal legend box, the bottom of the figure carries a terse caption:  
     “Plane 2D cutting areas, dashed = stressed form, filled region = relaxed form.”  
   – This makes clear that the dashed and solid outlines refer to the two states of each panel.  

 • Purpose and context  
   – In the TEXTILE workflow, curved patches defined by geodetic mesh lines are “ironed” into a 2D plane; the dashed outlines show that exact flattening, while the smaller filled polygons show how the textile relaxes once its shear stresses vanish.  
   – By printing both areas (3D versus 2D ironed versus 2D relaxed), the software verifies that the ironed 2D panels carry the same total area as the original curved surface (and quantifies the drop in area upon relaxation).  
   – The radial “explosion factor” is adjustable in the accompanying visualization tool (WINGRAF), so users can spread the pieces farther apart or draw them closer together as needed.  

Taken together, the image provides an at‐a‐glance check that (1) all pieces have been flattened without overlap, (2) the area conservation between original and ironed forms holds, and (3) the expected shrinkage on relaxation is correctly captured for every panel.

The illustration consists of two side-by-side 3D renderings of the same quadrilateral surface: on the left, the undeveloped “as-cut” shape in its original curved form; on the right, the same surface after being “ironed” or pressed into the plane (with a small explosion offset so individual elements do not overlap). Both views use a structured quadrilateral mesh with superimposed geodetic gridlines and show the location of boundary nodes.

Left half (original 3D cutting area)  
• Shape: A four-sided curved “cap” or dome, gently bulging upward. From this oblique vantage the near edges appear horizontal, the far edges curve away from the viewer in depth and height.  
• Color mapping: The surface is bi-colored down the mid-surface “seam.” The left-hand patch is rendered in a deep royal blue; the right-hand patch in a bright crimson red. Together they accentuate how the mesh transitions smoothly across the seam but remains topologically one continuous surface.  
• Mesh: A regular grid of isoparametric lines (light gray or white) overlays the colored patches, dividing the surface into small quadrilateral “rhombi.” These represent the finite-element or textile mesh used for development.  
• Boundary constraints: Along every edge of the surface small red markers (solid spheres) indicate fixed or supported nodes—points that will be held in place during the flattening process.

Right half (flattened 2D development)  
• Shape: The once-curved cap has been pressed nearly flat, yet retains slight elevation differences along one axis. Visually it splits into two horizontal “plates,” one set of elements remaining at a higher level, the adjacent set dropped to a lower level—creating a visible step. This reflects the relaxed (“membrane”) configuration under zero shear stiffness.  
• Color mapping: The entire mesh is shown in a uniform light cyan or aqua, emphasizing that no color‐based data mapping is present here—only the mesh topology matters.  
• Mesh and nodes: The quadrilateral grid remains intact, with mesh lines crisply overlaying each element. The same red boundary spheres mark the outer nodes, now lying in a single plane (aside from the step).  
• Explosion plot: The two halves of the mesh have been slightly separated (“exploded”) so that individual elements are clearly visible and do not overlap in the projection. This makes it easy to compare element shapes before and after flattening.  

Overall presentation  
• Viewpoint: Both halves are rendered from the same camera angle—slightly above and to the left—so that one can visually track how each mesh quadrilateral distorts when the 3D surface is laid out in 2D.  
• Purpose: The figure demonstrates TEXTILE’s ability to convert arbitrarily curved surfaces into developable 2D patches by exploiting the notion of geodetic lines and by controlling the mesh’s shear stiffness. It also visually validates that the ironed-out 2D area equals the original 3D surface area (no area change), even though a fully relaxed membrane area (not shown) would shrink.  
• Annotation: Below the rendering, the caption “Figure 2.5: Pressing down the 3D area into plane (first left cutting area)” affirms that this is the first of possibly several cutting-area examples.

Now the 3D cutting areas have to be developed into a 2D plane. This is the main task of TEXTILE. This ironing or polishing will cause additional strains and stresses in the material. These stresses depend on the shear stiffness of the textile material. Without shear stiffness nearly every 3D surface can be developed into plane by creating rhombus meshes. Now the sense of the geodetic lines appears: an area defined with geodetic lines can be developed as a rather straight area, although it appears like a curved banana in 3D (areas in the left lower region of the previous picture).
 In this picture the cutting areas are moved in plane as in an explosion plot to avoid overlapping. The explosion factor can be adjusted in WINGRAF.

In the relaxation step, the material shrinks to a stressfree area. As a textile has a huge nonlin- ear material behaviour, different compensation methods are available in program TEXTILE:
 1. Without further input the material shrinks according to the prestress and the linear material parameters.
 2. Independant of the prestress a constant compensation strain can be defined in warp and fill direction.
 3. 1+2: In addition to the linear material prestress strain an additive compensation strain can be defined.
 For the elastic prestress strain, separate material parameters can be set.
 5. For stress relations N-warp/N-fill the compenstion matrix can be defined. According to the actual stress in the current finite element a warp/fill compenstion strain eps- warp/eps-fill can be computed. With these matrix input the nonlinear behaviour of the compensation can be solved exactly.

The illustration is composed of two side-by-side schematic panels, each showing a flattened 2D cutting area of a tensile textile membrane. Both panels share the same basic rectangular footprint, a fine background grid of evenly spaced horizontal and vertical dashed lines, and two differently colored outlines: magenta for the stress-loaded (“stressed”) geometry and green for the shape after stress relief (“relaxed”).

Left Panel (without DECO)  
• The outer boundary is traced in magenta, indicating the target shape when the membrane is tensioned in its final 3D form.  
• Nested just inside the magenta line, a parallel green outline shows the projection of the same boundary after full relaxation (no added material). The green trace runs slightly inward from the magenta on most edges, reflecting the fabric’s elastic shrinkage once the tension is removed.  
• Along the top and bottom edges, the magenta and green lines are almost parallel and straight. The bottom edge shows a minor downward slope left to right, mirrored by the relaxed outline.  
• The left and right ends are squared off; the green line hugs slightly inside the magenta at each corner.  
• Behind both outlines, a regular grid of black dashed lines marks seam-and-cable-attachment locations in the fill (horizontal) and warp (vertical) directions. This makes clear that deformations are not uniform across the surface.

Right Panel (with DECO)  
• Again, a magenta outer shape represents the stressed boundary. It remains almost identical to the left panel’s magenta outline.  
• The green relaxed outline now includes a “DECO zone” at the downstream end (right-hand side). In this zone, the green line converges gradually toward the magenta, indicating that a linearly decreasing amount of compensation has been applied over the last few meters.  
• A cross-hatched “X” of dotted lines spans the DECO region near the left end of the panel, highlighting the transition area where compensation tapers off.  
• Vertical dashed seam lines remain visible, but the relaxed edge inside them is less offset from the stressed edge than in the non-DECO case.  
• Caption beneath reads: “Figure 2.6: Magenta = stressed, green = relaxed. Left without DECO, right with DECO.”

Overall, the figure demonstrates how introducing a controlled partial decompensation (DECO) in the fill direction on the final cutting segment reduces the mismatch between 3D tensioned and 2D flattened edges. The default edge-length control (EDGE = 0.50) ensures that once DECO is applied, the final relaxed outline more closely shares the stressed contour, minimizing excess material at seams and cable attachments.

Near the boundary cables and at the seam lines not the full compensation of the undistorted textile can be taken into account. One reason is, that in practice it is often not possible to stress the membrane tangetial to the stressed stiff boundary cable. Another reason is the higher stiffness at the seam lines.
 This effect called decompensation must be equalized by adding material at the end of the cloth width. This is the reason why always both the stressed and the stressfree 2D areas are plotted!
 With CUTT DECO... DECL... a linear decreasing relaxation in fill direction can be defined on the last DECL meters of the cutting areas. The region can be plotted in WINGRAF via ”structure of 2D-cutting areas”. Example: compare created areas with/without DECO in tex- tile4_cutting_via_elements.dat).
 But DECO has only little effect if EDGE>=0 is used. EDGE can control the edge length much more effective. Then DECO has only an effect on the inner membrane area (beside the edge).
 Default is EDGE 0.50. Then the flattened edge has just the same length as in the 3D system. After the compensation it gets a bit shorter due to the reduced compensation (factor 0.5).

The image is a WINGRAF plot of a ring-shaped assembly of two-dimensional cutting areas, each rendered as a triangular‐meshed panel with an overlaid warp‐direction indicator. Taken together, the panels form a nearly complete annulus, with a circular void in the center. Each panel is a trapezoidal or wedge-shaped finite‐element patch, outlined in two colors: a solid green line marks the element boundaries and a dashed magenta line draws an offset “stress‐free” outline around each patch. Within every patch the underlying finite‐element mesh is shown in light gray, with straight-line segments connecting nodes to form triangular elements.

Superimposed upon the mesh of each patch are short red dashes, all parallel within the same patch, denoting the computed warp direction for that area (in this sample the program’s default principal‐axis method was used, so the red lines point along each patch’s longer geometric axis). These red line segments are evenly spaced throughout the interior of each patch, providing a clear visual cue to the local warp orientation.

Overprinted in blue text near the midpoint of each wedge is a label of the form “Nr = X,” where X is an integer identifier (for example, panels labeled Nr = 8, Nr = 20, Nr = 2, Nr = 29, Nr = 18, Nr = 11, Nr = 28, Nr = 22, etc.). The sequence of these labels proceeds around the ring in ascending or descending order, indicating the numbering of cutting areas.

The entire arrangement is rendered against a plain white background. A caption below the plot reads “Figure 2.7: Warp direction in the 2D stressfree cutting areas.” Visually, the viewer’s eye is drawn first to the red warp‐direction lines, then to the regular triangular gray mesh, and finally to the colored outlines and blue labels that identify each wedge. The circular symmetry of the layout emphasizes that each patch has its own locally computed principal axis, even though all derive from the same global cutting geometry.

For the development of surface and the compensation the definition of the warp direction is very important. For this reason different methods to describe warp direction are available in TEXTILE:
 1. By default the program calculates the principal axis for the 2D cutting area and sets the warp direction into the longer axis.
 2. If the 2D-area is ”compact” and no clear principal axis can be extracted, the program takes the average of the original finite element coordination systems. This averaged local x axis will then be taken as warp direction for all elements of this cutting area.
 For special purpose a fixed angle in X-Y space can be defined for each cutting area.
 In the current sample the default had been used. The warp direction can be plotted with a red line in WINGRAF:

 Then best move the file $(name)_cutting_areas_mm.dxf from the explorer into the Autocad Window
 With SYST STOR ACAD also a .dxf file of the complete 3D mesh lines can be created, e.g. also with columns and walls.

The input is made in the CADINP language (see general manual SOFiSTiK: ’FEA / STRUC- TURAL Installation and Basics’). Three categories of units are distinguished:
 mm Fixed unit. Input is always required in the specified unit.
 [mm] Explicit unit. Input defaults to the specified unit. Alternatively, an explicit as- signment of a related unit is possible (eg. 2.5[m] ).

Below is a detailed, RAG-ready description of the table you provided. It defines six SOFiSTiK input records (CUTT, GRP, QUAD, COMP, LINE and ECHO) and the fields (items) associated with each.  The records HEAD, END and PAGE are referenced in the general SOFiSTiK manual (“FEA/STRUCTURAL Installation and Basics”) and so are not repeated here.

1. Record CUTT  
   • Purpose: Defines a “cutting” or sectioning operation within a model, often used to extract or project internal data.  
   • Items:  
     – NO   : Identifier number of the cut operation  
     – LC   : Load Case to which the cut refers  
     – MNO  : Master element or reference number (e.g. plate or volume element)  
     – LOCX : Local coordinate system number for projection  
     – PROJ : Projection type code (e.g. normal, tangent)

2. Record GRP  
   • Purpose: Defines or modifies a group of elements, nodes or lines; used for organizing and selecting sets.  
   • Items:  
     – NO  : Group number (unique identifier)  
     – VAL : Group value flag (e.g. ON=1/OFF=0 or a parameter setting)  

3. Record QUAD  
   • Purpose: Specifies a range of something (elements, time steps, etc.) in a “from–to–inc” format.  
   • Items:  
     – FROM : Starting index or value  
     – TO   : Ending index or value  
     – INC  : Increment step between successive values  

4. Record COMP  
   • Purpose: Defines a composite or combined definition, for example combining results or inputs from multiple components.  
   • Items:  
     – TYP  : Composite type code (e.g. SUM, MAX, USER‐DEFINED)  
     – N    : Number of entries (count of W-fields used)  
     – W1–W10: Weighting factors or references to component records; up to ten distinct entries  

5. Record LINE  
   • Purpose: Introduces a straight line in 3D space, typically used to define beam axes, cutting paths or graphic elements.  
   • Items:  
     – XA, YA, ZA : Coordinates of the line’s start point A in global system  
     – XE, YE, ZE : Coordinates of the line’s end point E in global system  
     – NX, NY, NZ : Optional direction cosines (unit vector components) of the line  
     – GRP        : Optional group number to which the line belongs  

6. Record ECHO  
   • Purpose: Controls echoing (on‐screen or listing output) of specific parameter settings or data lines.  
   • Items:  
     – OPT : Echo option code (e.g. ALL, NONE, SELECTIVE)  
     – VAL : Value or flag governing the echo (e.g. TRUE/FALSE or numeric level)  

Usage Notes  
• Each record begins in column 1 with the record name (e.g. “CUTT”) and may be continued over subsequent lines if more items are required.

The input table defines a very compact two‐row schema that exposes how to specify and parameterize a set of “control options” (OPT) and their corresponding values (VAL) for a cutting-and-flattening workflow. It is intended to be consumed by a calling program or script (e.g. via a Retrieval-Augmented Generation system or direct file parsing) to configure group selection, neighbor‐edge adjustment, and optional storage of animation load cases. Below is a breakdown of its structure and semantics:

1. Table Structure  
   • Columns  
     – Item: The name of the parameter or keyword (OPT, VAL).  
     – Description: A textual explanation of what that parameter controls or represents, including sub-options.  
     – Unit: Indicates the expected data type or unit of measure. Here “LIT” means a literal keyword or string, whereas “—” means “not applicable” or “unitless.”  
     – Default: The default setting, if no explicit value is provided. A hyphen (“–”) signals “no default.”  

   • Rows  
     – Row 1 (OPT): Introduces the control parameter name. Sub-entries in the Description cell explain available modes or flags that can be used once you specify OPT.  
     – Row 2 (VAL): Specifies that VAL holds the actual argument or data for whichever OPT has been chosen.  

2. OPT (Control option)  
   Unit: LIT  
   Default: – (no implicit default; you must specify both OPT and VAL to have an effect)  
   The Description cell lists three distinct sub-options you can select as the keyword assigned to OPT:  
     • GRP – Group selection option. When you choose CTRL GRP, you control which element groups get used or stored in the cutting analysis.  
         · CTRL GRP 2: Only elements belonging to the groups defined by GRP are actually cut; the cutting areas (from the WING data source) are applied only to those elements.  
         · CTRL GRP 3: All elements are cut (i.e. the same cutting areas are used on everything), but only those belonging to the selected GRP groups are kept in the flattened output. A canonical use case is trimming window openings in a roof plane.  
         · Example invocation:  
             CTRL GRP 3 GRP (200 225 1) cutt  
     • ADJU – Edge adjustment. A toggle for whether to modify the shared edges between neighboring cut areas.  
         · ADJU=0: Do not adjust edge boundaries (preserve original mesh connectivity).  
         · ADJU=1: Apply an automatic smoothing/realignment to adjacent cut outlines. This is also the default for ADJU.  
     • STOR – Storage of animation load cases. By specifying STOR and then setting VAL to “+8,” you instruct the system to include all animation load case data (e.g. from textile_animation.dat) in the flattened output.  

3. VAL (Value of the option)  
   Unit: —  
   Default: –  
   VAL holds the parameter or numeric/string value corresponding to whichever OPT keyword you have issued. Depending on the OPT choice, VAL may be:  
     • An integer code (2 or 3 for GRP modes)  
     • A tuple or list of group IDs (e.g. “(200 225 1)”)  
     • A Boolean flag (0 or 1 for ADJU)  
     • A bit mask or additive flag (e.g. “+8” for STOR)  

4. Usage Pattern in a Configuration File or Command Sequence  
   1. Specify a control keyword (OPT) followed by its option name (GRP, ADJU, or STOR).  
   2. On the next line or same line (depending on parser rules), assign VAL to the required argument for that option.  
   3. The program reads OPT to discover which sub-option to activate, then consumes VAL accordingly.  
   4. If ADJU is not explicitly set, ADJU defaults to 1 (edge adjustment on). GRP and STOR have no defaults and must be provided explicitly if needed.

By structuring the table this way, the software’s configuration remains both extensible (new OPT keywords can be added as new rows) and self-documenting (unit and default columns call out expected data types and fallback behaviors). This concise schema facilitates automated ingestion into a RAG vector store, where each Item-Description-Unit-Default quadruple can be tokenized, embedded, and retrieved to support downstream schema-aware prompts and code generation.

The table shown defines the input fields available under the CUTT (cutting‐area) command in the TEXTILE module for fabric shape development and compensation cutting. Each row corresponds to one keyword (Item), explains its role (Description), and—where applicable—gives its unit and default value. Together, these parameters govern how two‐dimensional membrane patches (“cutting areas”) are extracted, oriented, compensated for material strain, and displayed. Below is a detailed, parameter-by-parameter account:

1. NO  
  • Description: Cutting‐area identifier. If cutting areas are imported directly from WINGRAF, specifying NO is optional. However, when multiple CUTT definitions are given, each may use a distinct NO to allow per‐area customization.  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: “–” (no default; inherited from WINGRAF when omitted)

2. LC  
  • Description: Load case number used to compute compensation (elastic strain recovery) in warp/fill directions. Required only when cutting areas are defined manually via element groups (GRP). If WINGRAF supplies the areas, LC is set there.  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: —

3. MNO  
  • Description: Material number for compensation. Use this to assign a separate material definition for linear compensation calculations (e.g. different elastic constants). If not specified, the primary membrane material is used.  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: —

4. LOCX  
  • Description: Local warp (X) axis orientation in the 2D flattening plane. By default, the principal axis of each patch (longer dimension) becomes warp. For “compact” shapes without a clear principal axis, an average of the original finite‐element local x‐axes is used. You may override this with a fixed XY rotation.  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: principal‐axis‐based

5. PROJ  
  • Description: Projection direction for surface development. If automatic projection fails (e.g. severely twisted patch), you can manually specify the direction with a literal triplet (XX, YY, ZZ) or oriented pairs (XYZ, XNYZ, etc.).  
  • Unit: LIT (literal vector)  
  • Default: automatic

6. DECO  
  • Description: Decompensation factor—reduces the relaxation allowance in the fill direction toward the patch ends. Generally has minor effect if EDGE≥0. Control edge compensation more effectively with EDGE.  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: —

7. DECL  
  • Description: Length (in meters) of the “end zone” where fill‐direction decompensation (DECO) applies. See sample textile1_tennishall.dat for typical usage.  
  • Unit: [m]  
  • Default: —

8. EDGE  
  • Description: Boundary‐edge strain control factor:  
    – EDGE = –1: edge‐length control off (outer edges expand freely)  
    – EDGE = 0.0: no relaxation allowed—flattened edge length equals 3D length (no stress during assembly)  
    – 0 < EDGE < 1: partial compensation—some assembly tension required (practical)  
    – EDGE = 1.0: full compensation—flattened edge shortest (difficult to assemble)  
    Default 0.5 typically models double‐layer hems or boundary cables restricting edge strain.  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: 0.5

9. EDGI  
  • Description: Same concept as EDGE but applied to inner (hole or cut‐out) edges within a patch.  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: 0.5

10. EXPO  
  • Description: “Explosion” factor for 2D plots. Offsets patches in the plane to prevent overlaps in graphical output. Can also be set in WINGRAF.  
  • Unit: —  
  • Default: 1.30

Notes on Workflow Integration  
- Mode 1 (WINGRAF-driven): Simply issue “CUTT” (no additional keywords) after WINGRAF export. All area definitions, LC and material references are inherited.  
- Mode 2 (Manual): Precede the CUTT command with “GRP” specifying element‐group IDs. Then define LC, MNO, LOCX, etc., explicitly.  
- To redefine or delete existing areas, use “CUTT NO –1,” which clears prior definitions so new numbering may be applied.  
- LOCX, PROJ and EDGE settings allow fine control over fabric orientation and assembly stresses, ensuring that the flattened patterns will install as intended under real‐world boundary conditions.

Below is a self-contained, RAG-ready description of the two-row parameter table you provided. It explains each field, its role, default, and how it ties into the broader cutting-area workflow (see also CUTT, QUAD, GRP and example TEXTILE3.dat).

1. Table purpose and context  
• This table defines two control items—NO and VAL—used when specifying group numbers for cutting areas.  
• It is part of a workflow that can either rely on WINGRAF definitions or, alternatively, directly invoke GRP (group) and QUAD (quadrant) entries to delimit cutting regions.  
• Typical usage appears in TEXTILE3.dat; if no WINGRAF blocks exist, GRP and QUAD sections in the same data file must supply the geometry.  

2. Column definitions  
• Item (string) – The mnemonic code identifying the parameter. Two codes are supported here: “NO” and “VAL.”  
• Description (string) – A human-readable explanation of what the parameter controls. Multiline text is used for VAL to list its three permitted sub-values (YES, NO, FULL).  
• Unit (string) – Always “–” (not applicable), since neither item takes a numeric or dimensional quantity.  
• Default (string) – The value assumed when the parameter is omitted in the input. For NO, there is no default; for VAL, the default mode is FULL.  

3. Row-by-row semantics  

A. Item = NO  
 ‑ Group number  
 ‑ This entry announces or reserves the identifier for the current group of cutting areas.  
 ‑ Unit: none  
 ‑ Default: “–” (no implicit group number is assigned if you omit NO; you must supply it explicitly when grouping is required).  

B. Item = VAL  
 ‑ Controls whether and how the group number defined by NO is applied during processing. It accepts exactly three keywords:  
    • YES – Enable the use of the group number. Internally, downstream routines will recognize and apply the group identifier but will not generate any explicit textual output of the group number in the result file.  
    • NO – Disable any grouping. The group number (if supplied via NO) is ignored, and no grouping logic is invoked.  
    • FULL – Fully enable grouping: the system applies the group number during internal computations and also emits the group number in the output.  
 ‑ Unit: none  
 ‑ Default: FULL (if VAL is omitted, the system assumes that you want full grouping behavior, with both internal use and output of the group number).  

4. How this ties into the broader cutting-area definitions  
• In routines like CUTT and when defining polygonal areas via QUAD, one often wants to collect subsets of polygons under a single “group number.”  
• By combining NO + VAL, you explicitly mark which polygons belong to which group and whether that grouping should propagate to the final output data set.  
• If you have already defined regions via WINGRAF blocks, you may not need NO/VAL at all; GRP/QUAD are the fallback mechanism when WINGRAF is absent.  

5. Example snippet (pseudocode from TEXTILE3.dat)  
    NO  5  
    VAL FULL  
    QUAD … (coordinates of cutting polygon)  
    QUAD … (further vertices)  
    ENDQUAD  

In this example, group number 5 is declared, grouping is fully active (internal and output), and the following QUAD blocks define the geometric boundaries. When the file is processed, any object inside that polygon inherits group 5, and the output will explicitly list “5” alongside the processed shapes.

The table below summarizes the three parameters used to define an element‐range for a QUAD (quadrilateral) group in TEDDY (often invoked via the “QUAD FROM” heading).  These parameters let you specify a contiguous block of element IDs by giving a start, an end, and a step size.  They are dimensionless integers, and each has a sensible default so that, if you only supply FROM, the command still works.

Table structure  
• Columns  
  – Item:     the keyword you must enter (“FROM”, “TO”, or “INC”)  
  – Description: what this keyword controls  
  – Unit:     always “–” (dimensionless, since these are just element ID counters)  
  – Default:  the value assumed if you omit this line  

• Rows  
  1. FROM  
     – Description: Start element number.  
     – Default: 1  
     – Notes: This is the lowest element ID in your selection.  If you omit TO and INC, only element 1 will be selected.  

  2. TO  
     – Description: End element number.  
     – Default: taken from the value you gave for FROM  
     – Notes: Since TO defaults to the same value as FROM, a minimal “single‐element” selection (FROM=5, TO=5) requires only one line in your QUAD bloc.  

  3. INC  
     – Description: Increment (step size) between successive element IDs.  
     – Default: 1  
     – Notes: A step of 1 picks every element in the range.  If you set INC=2, you select every second element (e.g. 1, 3, 5, …).  

Typical workflow in TEDDY with ANIMATOR  
  1. In ANIMATOR, open the Reduce → Select Elements menu.  
  2. Hold the CTRL key and click or drag to add individual elements or ranges interactively.  
  3. Right-click and choose “Copy selection to clipboard.”  
  4. Back in TEDDY, use “Include from clipboard” (or simply press CTRL-V) to paste the list of IDs.  
  5. Prepend a single heading line:  
       QUAD FROM  
     This tells TEDDY you are starting a QUAD block with explicit FROM/TO/INC entries.  
  6. Paste the three‐column table you prepared (or generated from ANIMATOR) immediately after that heading.  

See also:  
  • GRP: for defining named groups of elements without specifying a continuous range.  
  • QUAD: the general command under which FROM/TO/INC operate.  
  • Example usage: see TEXTILE4.dat for a sample input file that combines GRP definitions with QUAD ranges.

The input table defines the syntax and meaning of each keyword and numeric field used to prescribe compensation strains in a finite-element membrane model.  It has four columns—Item, Description, Unit and Default—and covers all six supported compensation methods: CE1, CE2, DE1, DE2, S1/S2 and E1/E2.  Below is a field-by-field breakdown with context from the underlying theoretical principles.  

1.  TYPE  
   • Description: Selects the compensation method.  
     – CE1, CE2: impose a constant pre-defined strain (independent of prestress) in warp (CE1) or fill (CE2) direction.  
     – DE1, DE2: add an extra strain on top of the linear prestress strain in warp (DE1) or fill (DE2) direction.  
     – S1, S2 & E1, E2: specify a full nonlinear compensation matrix that relates actual in-plane stresses (warp/fill) to warp/fill compensation strains.  
   • Unit: LIT (literal code)  
   • Default: “!” (mandatory keyword)  

2.  N  
   • Description:  
     – For matrix methods S1 and S2: total number of columns (for S1) or rows (for S2) in the compensation matrix.  These define the stress breakpoints at which the compensation strains are tabulated.  
     – For matrix methods E1 and E2: the specific row index in the matrix to which the following W-values apply.  Rows correspond to discrete fill-direction stress levels.  
   • Unit: none (integer count)  
   • Default: “–” (no built-in default)  

3.  W1  
   • Description: varies by method:  
     – DE1/DE2: the additional strain (%) to be added to the prestress strain in the warp (DE1) or fill (DE2) direction.  
     – S1/S2: the stress value (in kN/m) that defines the first column (S1) or first row (S2) of the matrix.  These are the stress breakpoints at which strains will be computed.  
     – E1/E2: the compensation strain (%) corresponding to the first column stress point of that row.  
   • Unit: “*” indicates percent for strains or kN/m for stresses as appropriate.  
   • Default: “–” (no default; must be supplied)  

4.  W2 … W10  
   • Description: Additional column entries following the same convention as W1.  In constant/additive methods these extra W-fields are unused.  In matrix methods they represent:  
     – For S1/S2: further stress breakpoints (columns of S1 or rows of S2).  You may specify up to nine additional stress values, making up to ten columns/rows total.  
     – For E1/E2: compensation strains corresponding to each successive stress breakpoint in that row.  Thus E1〈row〉 W1–W10 are the warp-direction strains at the defined column stresses; E2〈row〉 W1–W10 likewise for the fill direction.  
   • Unit: same as W1 (“*”)  
   • Default: “–”  

How this ties into the theoretical principles:  
– Methods CE1/CE2 correspond to “case 2” in the theory: a constant compensation strain independent of prestress.  
– Methods DE1/DE2 are “case 3,” adding a constant offset to the linear prestress strain.  
– Methods S1/S2 combined with E1/E2 realize “case 4,” where a full nonlinear stress-to-strain compensation mapping is defined.  S1 and S2 declare the discrete warp and fill stress levels, and the E-tables give the warp/fill strain responses at each stress-pair grid point.  
– During analysis, the algorithm locates the appropriate column (warp stress via S1) and row (fill stress via S2) and reads E1/E2 at that intersection.  If the actual element stresses fall between tabulated points, linear interpolation is used to compute the precise compensation strains.  

No field in this table carries an internal default; every entry must be provided to fully define the compensation behavior for the chosen TYPE.

Below is a self-contained, detailed description of the 4×4 “matrix compensation” table.  It associates a pair of compensation strains—warp‐direction (ε₁) and fill-direction (ε₂)—with discrete values of membrane force in the warp (columns) and fill (rows) directions.  This table corresponds to “mode 4” in the COMP definitions (COMP S1/S2 for selecting column/row indices and COMP E1/E2 for the actual strain values).

1. Coordinate Axes  
   – Columns (warp‐force index, selected by COMP S1):  
     • Column 1 → N_warp = 0.0 kN/m  
     • Column 2 → N_warp = 1.0 kN/m  
     • Column 3 → N_warp = 4.0 kN/m  
     • Column 4 → N_warp = 10.0 kN/m  
   – Rows (fill‐force index, selected by COMP S2):  
     • Line 1 → N_fill = 0.0 kN/m  
     • Line 2 → N_fill = 1.0 kN/m  
     • Line 3 → N_fill = 4.0 kN/m  
     • Line 4 → N_fill = 10.0 kN/m  

2. Cell Contents (ε₁=warp compensation, ε₂=fill compensation)  
   – Row 1 (N_fill=0.0 kN/m):  
     • Col 1 (N_warp=0.0):  ε₁=3.0 %, ε₂=3.0 %  
     • Col 2 (N_warp=1.0):  ε₁=4.0 %, ε₂=2.0 %  
     • Col 3 (N_warp=4.0):  ε₁=4.5 %, ε₂=1.0 %  
     • Col 4 (N_warp=10.0): ε₁=5.0 %, ε₂=0.0 %  
   – Row 2 (N_fill=1.0 kN/m):  
     • Col 1:  ε₁=2.0 %, ε₂=4.0 %  
     • Col 2:  ε₁=3.2 %, ε₂=3.2 %  
     • Col 3:  ε₁=3.6 %, ε₂=2.0 %  
     • Col 4:  ε₁=4.3 %, ε₂=1.0 %  
   – Row 3 (N_fill=4.0 kN/m):  
     • Col 1:  ε₁=1.0 %, ε₂=4.5 %  
     • Col 2:  ε₁=2.0 %, ε₂=3.5 %  
     • Col 3:  ε₁=2.8 %, ε₂=2.8 %  
     • Col 4:  ε₁=3.6 %, ε₂=2.0 %  
   – Row 4 (N_fill=10.0 kN/m):  
     • Col 1:  ε₁=0.0 %, ε₂=5.0 %  
     • Col 2:  ε₁=1.0 %, ε₂=4.3 %  
     • Col 3:  ε₁=2.0 %, ε₂=3.6 %  
     • Col 4:  ε₁=3.0 %, ε₂=3.0 %  

3. Usage Example  
   If at a given point the computed membrane forces are  
     N_warp = 10 kN/m → selects Column 4  
     N_fill = 4 kN/m → selects Line 3  
   then the lookup yields  
     ε₁ (warp) = 3.6 %  (from COMP E1 at row 3, col 4)

4. Interpolation

This record, known as LINE, defines one individual cutting‐line segment for use by the WINGRAF/SOFIPLUS system.  In practice it appears in batch runs (for example in TEXTILE1.dat) or may be created interactively.  After LINE records are in place, a subsequent WINGRAF session will convert them into true geodetic (surface–shortest) or fixed (straight in plan) lines and then compute the full 3D cutting areas.  For reference to the mathematical underpinnings, see “TheoreticalPrinciples.”

1. Coordinate Endpoints  
   • XA, YA, ZA: Cartesian coordinates (in metres) of the segment’s start point.  No default values—each must be supplied.  
   • XE, YE, ZE: Cartesian coordinates (in metres) of the segment’s end point.  Also mandatory, with no defaults.

2. Projection Direction  
   • NX, NY, NZ: A directional vector defining the projection orientation of this cutting line.  These components are dimensionless.  If not otherwise specified, the default direction is (0, 0, 1), meaning a projection straight down the Z‐axis.  You may alter one or more of these components to tilt the cutting plane in space.

3. Group Mask  
   • GRP: An optional “element group” filter.  If provided, the cutting operation acts only on the specified group.  If omitted or set to “–,” the line will apply to all geometry groups.  No numerical default is used by convention.

4. Line Type  
   • TYPE: A text flag that determines how the line is interpreted geodetically:  
       – GEOD: The system will treat the segment as a true geodetic (shortest‐path) line on the surface.  Under the hood, WINGRAF adjusts the raw XY endpoints so the line follows terrain curvature, then extrudes the cutting plane accordingly.  
       – FIX: The system treats the endpoints as fixed in the ground (plan) view.  No surface‐conforming adjustment is made; the cut remains straight in the XY plane.  
     No default is assumed; you must explicitly choose either GEOD or FIX.

Usage Notes  
   – Typical datasets include multiple LINE records defining an entire cutting layout.  They may be pre‐defined in batch files or drawn interactively in the graphical modules of WINGRAF or SOFIPLUS.  
   – After batch definition, simply launch WINGRAF on the same project: the software automatically reads all LINE records, computes the adjusted 3D geodetic or fixed lines, and generates the full 3D cutting areas for further processing or visualization.  
   – For a complete walkthrough and mathematical justification (how GEOD lines follow shortest‐path solutions on complex surfaces versus FIX lines), see the section “Theoretical Background.”  
   – Example files “TEXTILE1.dat,” “Example1,” and “Example2” illustrate simple and advanced usages of all LINE parameters.

The table defines two related parameters—OPT and VAL—that together control how “cutting‐area” coordinates are emitted into an output file.  They appear in the context of an “ECHO LIST YES” command (or its post‐run equivalent) which instructs the system to produce a list of all cutting‐area coordinates.

1. Item: OPT  
   • Description: This field selects which “echo” option to invoke. It must be one of the literals in the supported list.  
     – LIST: Request the coordinate list of all cutting areas.  
   • Unit: LIT (i.e. a literal keyword)  
   • Default: – (no default value; OPT must be explicitly provided)  

   Explanation:  
   OPT serves as the keyword that identifies the type of information you want echoed.  In the current implementation, only a single keyword—LIST—is valid.  When you set OPT to LIST, the system knows you are asking for the complete set of cutting‐area coordinates to be written out.

2. Item: VAL  
   • Description: Defines the verbosity or extent of the output once an option is activated.  The valid literal values are:  
     – OFF: Completely deactivate the option (no echo, even if OPT is specified).  
     – NO: Keep the option “on” but suppress all output (effectively a silent mode).  
     – YES: Produce the standard, regular output.  
     – FULL: Produce extensive output, including additional details beyond the standard set.  
     – EXTR: Produce extreme output—i.e., maximal detail, potentially including debug-level or diagnostic information.  
   • Unit: LIT (i.e. a literal keyword)  
   • Default: FULL  

   Explanation:  
   VAL modulates how much information you actually receive once the option has been turned on.  Its default is FULL, meaning that if you issue “ECHO LIST” without explicitly specifying VAL, the system will generate extensive information about each cutting area.  If you want less or more detail, you can override it by appending NO, YES or EXTR.

Overall Usage Example  
  To request a standard list of all cutting‐area coordinates:  
    ECHO LIST YES  

  To suppress output completely (even though you requested the list):  
    ECHO LIST OFF  

  To get the most verbose, diagnostic‐level listing:  
    ECHO LIST EXTR  

Post-run Invocation  
  The same command can be issued after the main run has completed, enclosed between HEAD and END markers:  
    HEAD  
    ECHO LIST YES  
    END  

This table thus encapsulates both what you can ask for (OPT = LIST) and how much of it you actually get (VAL = OFF/NO/YES/FULL/EXTR), with sensible defaults to guarantee that, in the absence of a VAL setting, you still receive full output.

  – The central opening has morphed into an elongated ellipse, also drawn in green. Two green diagonals across this ellipse indicate principal element directions or stiffening lines within the perforation boundary.

• Load‐vector directions and geodesic cutting lines  
  – Radiating in red from the boundary toward the opening— and vice versa—are straight lines whose orientation is normal to the deformed surface. These either show the load vectors computed on the deformed mesh (as described in load case 2) or, equivalently, the geodetic “cutting lines” generated by WINGRAF for pattern development.  
  – The red rays are regularly spaced around the opening, illustrating the subdivision into narrow 3D‐cutting strips that will later be developed into 2D panels.

• Local element coordinate axes  
  – Along the edge of the oval aperture appear many short black line segments (ticks). Each one denotes an element’s local x–y axes (warp and fill directions). Their orientation relative to the global system highlights areas where the material’s principal directions diverge from the computed geodesic lines—exactly the discrepancy the program warns about if local element axes aren’t rotated to align with the strip orientation.

• Layering of results  
  – By showing the original mesh, the green deformed form-found shape, the red load/geodesic lines, and the black local axes together, the figure conveys the full sequence:  
    1. Start with a planar mesh under vertical z-direction loading.  
    2. Compute the prestressed, form-found geometry via inner pressure (load case 2).  
    3. Reapply the load vectors normal to that deformed shape.  
    4. Extract geodesic lines for cutting‐pattern generation.  
    5. Visualize local axes to verify material alignment.

This layered visualization is exactly what a TEXTILE + WINGRAF workflow produces: it confirms the form-found geometry, defines the true loading direction on the deformed surface, and lays out the geodesic cutting strips—ready for 2D development and compensation steps.

Description of geometry and mesh

The mesh lines are drawn in dark gray, crisply dividing the panels into equal cells.  

Color shading and lighting

Contextual annotations and caption

The image (labelled “Figure 4.12: Development of surface in six virtual steps, 3D view”) is a 2-by-3 array of wire-frame mesh renderings, each showing the incremental unfolding of a three-quadrant, right-angled surface into a flat cutting pattern. All meshes are drawn in thin blue lines on a plain white background and are presented from a consistent, slightly elevated oblique viewpoint.

Layout and sequence  
• The six views are arranged in two columns and three rows.  
• The left column illustrates development steps 1, 3 and 5; the right column shows steps 2, 4 and 6.  
• Time (or step number) increases first down the left column, then continues down the right.

Mesh topology  
• Each mesh is composed of uniform quadrilateral cells (grid lines), corresponding to a total original area of three 10 m × 10 m squares (300 m²).  
• The original L-shaped surface is formed by two orthogonally hinged panels: one vertical and one horizontal, each subdivided into a regular grid.  
• Adjacencies and edge connections remain constant throughout all steps.

Step-by-step description  
1. Step 1 (top left): The surface is in its original configuration. A flat horizontal panel (floor) is laid out in front, while a connected vertical panel (wall) rises sharply at a right angle from its back edge. The mesh lines form perfect squares aligned to principal horizontal and vertical axes.  
2. Step 2 (top right): The vertical panel has begun to rotate downward about the hinge line, now tilting toward the viewer. The angle between panels is less than 90°, and the mesh squares on both panels remain undeformed but are viewed in perspective.  
3. Step 3 (middle left): Further unfolding has occurred. The former wall panel swings below horizontal, creating a shallow obtuse angle with the original floor. The grid still shows crisp right angles at each quad, but two panels now lie in different but nearly coplanar planes.  
4. Step 4 (middle right): The boundary between panels is almost flat. Only a slight kink remains at the former hinge. All quads continue to appear rectangular, though foreshortening in perspective hints at the last vestige of 3D curvature.  
5. Step 5 (bottom left): Virtually all bending has been removed; the mesh looks almost entirely planar. A subtle bulge at what was originally the panel junction indicates residual strain, but topologically the surface is now a single contiguous patch.  
6. Step 6 (bottom right): Fully developed state. The mesh has been relaxed into a flat, nearly perfect rectangle. The uniform quad pattern shows very minor stretching (area_2D = 300.027 m² vs. original 300.000 m²), demonstrating minimal distortion during flattening.

Overall, this six-panel graphic succinctly visualizes how a compound, right-angled surface composed of three 10 × 10 m quadrats can be “unfolded” step by step into a single flat cutting pattern. The consistent wire-frame style emphasizes topology and area preservation—key data that underpin the TEXTILE module’s reported development results.

The image (Figure 4.13) shows the flattened “cutting pattern” or ground‐view development of a doubly curved 3D surface. Rendered entirely in thin blue wireframe lines on a white background, it consists of a regular quadrilateral mesh that has been relaxed and laid out in the plane without appreciable area loss. Key visual elements and their meanings are:  

1. Overall Shape  
   • The outline is a single contiguous region shaped roughly like a tapered fan or teardrop:  
     – A sharp “pivot” or tip at the left-hand side where three original 10 m × 10 m quadrats met.  
     – Two smooth, gently curved long edges sweeping outward and to the right, forming a broad arc on the right.  
     – Slight symmetry about a horizontal centerline, reflecting the original 3-quadrat arrangement.  

2. Quadrilateral Mesh  
   • The interior is filled with a grid of quadrilaterals, each originally a 10 × 10 m patch in 3D.  
   • Lines radiate somewhat from the tip and also form near-concentric bands, indicating how the surface stretches and rotates as it is unrolled.  
   • Near the center (left tip), quads are more regularly square; farther out toward the broad right edge they become slightly skewed and stretched, showing the material’s relaxation.  

3. Boundary Behavior  
   • The two long edges are not straight: each is a smooth curve whose curvature corresponds to the original surface’s curvature in 3D (one edge bending slightly concave, the other convex).  
   • The outermost row of quads is marginally larger and less uniform, evidence of slight tensile adjustment in the development process.  

4. Scale and Area Preservation  
   • Despite small local distortions, the listing in the accompanying TEXTILE output confirms that the total 2D developed area is 300.027 m² versus the original 300.000 m² in 3D—an imperceptible 0.027 m² difference over three 10 × 10 m patches.  
   • The uniform grid spacing (thin blue lines) visually reinforces that the mesh has been “relaxed” to minimize internal stresses.  

5. Purpose and Context  
   • This view is one of six frames in a sequence showing progressive flattening of a 3D area comprised of three quadrats.  
   • Displacements from the original geometry are stored under load case 1001 and can be replayed in an animator to verify the cut pattern before actual textile or sheet‐metal fabrication.  

In sum, the image documents the successful planar development of a moderately curved, three-panel surface: a precise wireframe representation of how the original 300 m² 3D region becomes a single flat cutting pattern with minimal distortion, ready for downstream manufacturing or pattern‐cutting operations.
